name: Naturalistic fallacy
statement: Moore's naturalistic fallacy is defining 'good' as some other property, and he brought the same charge against definitions drawn from a supersensible reality.
meaning: The name is G. E. Moore's and the claim is narrower than the name suggests. Moore held that 'good' denotes a simple quality which cannot be analysed into anything else. The mistake he named is committed by a philosopher who identifies some other property that all good things share, and then treats that property as what 'good' means. Moore writes that too many philosophers have thought that when they named those other properties they were actually defining good, and that those properties were 'absolutely and entirely the same with goodness'. His next sentence is the naming: 'This view I propose to call the naturalistic fallacy.' The word 'natural' in that phrase is a technical term of Moore's own. He defines nature as 'that which is the subject-matter of the natural sciences and also of psychology', and says it 'may be said to include all that has existed, does exist, or will exist in time'. So pleasure, desire and social approval are natural properties in his sense. This atlas covers the everyday inference from natural to good under appeal to nature, which is a measured preference rather than a claim about definition. It covers Hume's is-ought passage there too, and this entry does not take that on. What the three share is a subject and not an argument.

origin.note: Moore names the fallacy in section 10 of chapter I and returns to it through the book. The text read here is the Project Gutenberg transcription of the 1922 reprint, whose front matter gives first edition 1903 and reprinted 1922, and whose preface is dated August 1903. Moore credits the indefinability of 'good' to Sidgwick in section 14, saying that so far as he knows only one ethical writer, Professor Henry Sidgwick, has clearly recognised and stated it, and citing the Methods of Ethics Book I chapter iii.

evidence: The case is textual, and the text is short on the point. Moore's illustration is yellow. Light vibrations of a certain kind correspond to yellow, and are not what yellow means, because we should never have found the vibrations had we not first noticed the difference between the colours. He says a mistake of this simple kind has commonly been made about 'good'. It may be true that all good things are also something else, and Ethics aims at discovering what those other properties are, and naming them is not defining good. Section 11 sets the dilemma. If 'good' just means the object of desire, then a philosopher who argues that the object of desire is not pleasure has proved a psychological point and no ethical one. Moore's own analogy is a man who says a triangle is a circle and a man who says it is a straight line, arguing past each other because each has defined the term his own way. The other branch is that the dispute is verbal, about which word most people use for what, which he says no exponent of naturalistic Ethics would accept as all he meant. Section 13 carries the argument the literature now calls the open question argument, a name Moore does not use. Take a proposed definition, that to be good is to be that which we desire to desire. Applied to a case the definition looks plausible. Then ask 'Is it good to desire to desire A?' and the question is as intelligible as the original 'Is A good?', which it would not be if the definition were correct, since the analysed version would run 'Do we desire to desire to desire to desire A?'. Moore's test is that anyone can convince himself by inspection that the predicate 'good' is positively different from 'desiring to desire'. His second target is the view that 'good' has no meaning at all, and there his point is that whoever asks 'Is pleasure after all good?' can satisfy himself that he is not merely wondering whether pleasure is pleasant. The phrase 'open question' appears four times in the Gutenberg text and never as the name of an argument. Two passages fix the scope. Section 25 divides the theories in two. One group defines good by a natural object, the other by an object inferred to exist in a supersensible real world. Of the second group Moore writes that 'the fallacy, by reference to which I define Metaphysical Ethics, is the same in kind; and I give it but one name, the naturalistic fallacy'. Section 26 gives the general form: whether good be defined as yellow or green or blue, as loud or soft, as round or square, as sweet or bitter, as productive of life or productive of pleasure, as willed or desired or felt, the theory which holds it to mean them will be a naturalistic theory. Moore also says the name does not matter to him. In section 12 he writes that the same confusion between two natural objects would not be called naturalistic. He adds that even if good were a natural object the nature and importance of the fallacy would be unaltered, and that 'I do not care about the name: what I do care about is the fallacy'. The everyday appeal to nature does appear, as one instance among many. Section 27 takes the maxim recommending a life according to nature and argues that 'natural' there can only mean normal, that the abnormal is often better than the normal, and that Socrates and Shakespeare were not normal. He closes it: 'We must not, therefore, be frightened by the assertion that a thing is natural into the admission that it is good; good does not, by definition, mean anything that is natural; and it is therefore always an open question whether anything that is natural is good.' Section 28 treats the second sense, in which natural means necessary, and says that when a bare minimum for life is recommended as the way of life to which Nature points her finger, the naturalistic fallacy is used.

replication.headline: No experiment on the open question argument, or on whether people treat evaluative and natural terms as synonymous, was found.
replication.detail: The search covered Crossref for the open question argument paired with experimental terms, for the naturalistic fallacy paired with experiments and participants, and for folk metaethics; OpenAlex on the same terms; and Europe PMC for the naturalistic fallacy with participants or experiment. Crossref returns philosophy chapters and commentary, most of them from Sinclair's 2018 Cambridge volume on the fallacy, and no study. Europe PMC's fifteen top hits are papers in medicine, sociology and education that use the phrase in passing. The nearest live empirical literature is folk metaethics, which asks whether people treat moral claims as objective rather than whether they treat 'good' as synonymous with any natural predicate. The Stanford Encyclopedia's entry on experimental moral philosophy was read in full and contains neither the phrase 'open question' nor 'naturalistic fallacy'; its five occurrences of Moore are all other authors of that surname. An absence of experiments is what should be expected here. Moore's claim is about what a word means and what follows from that, and the test he proposes is one a reader runs on himself by inspection, which is a report about competent speakers rather than a prediction about a sample.

limits: Frankena's article was not obtained. Oxford holds it closed, Unpaywall returns no open location, and no repository copy exists. Its record was verified at Crossref for title, author, volume, issue, pages and year. Everything attributed to it here comes from two documents that quote it with page numbers: Michael Ridge's Stanford Encyclopedia entry, and William Piervincenzi's 2007 Rochester doctoral thesis, which devotes a chapter to it and disagrees with it. One page cite in that thesis, 272-73, falls outside the article's range of 464-477 and appears to be a slip for 472-73. The reading of Moore here rests on one transcription of one printing. The Gutenberg text is the 1922 reprint, and Moore wrote a preface for a second edition that he never published, which the thesis quotes from a later edition that was not consulted. Moore's 1942 reply to his critics was likewise not read, so this page says nothing about whether he later changed his mind. Curry's survey is used only for the range of things the name is applied to. His readings of Moore are contested and not adopted here, and one of them, that for Moore the opposite of natural is intuitive rather than supernatural, sits badly with Moore's own section 25, which contrasts natural objects with objects inferred to exist in a supersensible real world. Lorraine Daston's article on the history of the term in Isis was located and is closed at the publisher; its green copy at the Max Planck repository returns 403, and nothing on this page rests on it. No systematic count of how the term is used in print exists, or at least none was found, so the claim about drift below is a claim about named instances rather than about frequency.
misreadings: The common reading is not Moore's. Popular fallacy references now lead with the inference from is to ought. Logically Fallacious describes the naturalistic fallacy as a conclusion expressing what ought to be, based only on what is, and files Moore's version second, as 'a more traditional use'. Curry set eight uses of the name side by side in 2006, each with a source: moving from is to ought, moving from facts to values, identifying good with its object, claiming that good is a natural property, going in the direction of evolution, assuming that what is natural is good, assuming that what currently exists ought to exist, and substituting explanation for justification. He quotes Dylan Evans for the sixth, that arguing something is good because it is natural is called the naturalistic fallacy, and David Buss for the seventh, that the fallacy maintains that whatever exists should exist. Curry's own summary is that the name has come to be synonymous with the belief that the natural and the normative inhabit two separate realms. Reference works have held the line better than the popular ones. English Wikipedia's article, which drew 44,259 views in 2025 by the Wikimedia pageviews API, opens with the definitional claim rather than the inferential one. The second error runs the other way, and treats the fallacy as an argument against naturalism. Moore charges metaphysical ethics with it as well, and Ridge concludes that the real target is reductionism rather than naturalism, since a naturalist who holds that moral properties are natural but irreducible is untouched. Ridge adds that the name is poorly named on a second count, because it is not really a fallacy. The charitable reading of 'X is pleasant, therefore X is good' supplies the suppressed premise that whatever is pleasant is good, and a non-naturalist can accept that premise while denying that it holds in virtue of an identity. Frankena is the source of that line of objection. Ridge reports his point that it cannot be assumed at the outset that what Moore calls the fallacy is a mistake of any kind, since a naturalist could then complain that the central question has been begged. Piervincenzi's account adds the detail. Frankena separates two uses. In one the charge is thrown at an opponent as though it settled the matter, and in the other it is applied after the argument has been made. He takes the first to be illegitimate, because the fallaciousness of the naturalistic fallacy is what is at issue. Frankena's own name for the mistake underneath it is the definist fallacy, which Piervincenzi quotes as the process of confusing or identifying two properties, of defining one property by another, or of substituting one property for another, so that the fallacy is always simply that two properties are being treated as one. The third error is to suppose that Moore had nothing to say about the everyday appeal to nature. He did, in sections 27 and 28, and his verdict there is that good does not by definition mean anything natural. The point is that this is one application of the fallacy and not its definition, and a reader who runs the two together will expect Moore's argument to work against natural remedies and find it working against hedonism instead.

sources.text: Moore, G. E. (1903). Principia Ethica. Cambridge University Press. Read in full as the Project Gutenberg transcription, ebook 53430, of the 1922 reprint of the first edition. The source for every quotation from Moore on this page, and for the count of occurrences of 'open question'.

Frankena, W. K. (1939). IV.-The Naturalistic Fallacy. Mind, XLVIII(192), 464-477. Verified at Crossref for title, author, volume, issue, pages and year. Closed at Oxford, no open location at Unpaywall, and not obtained. It is described here only as Ridge and Piervincenzi describe it.

Ridge, M. Moral Non-Naturalism. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, first published 1 February 2003, substantive revision 14 June 2025. Read in full from the page source. The source for the open question argument as the literature states it, for the charge that the name is poorly named on two counts, and for Frankena's question-begging objection.

Piervincenzi, W. (2007). G.E. Moore's Naturalistic Fallacy and Open Question Argument Reconsidered. Doctoral thesis, University of Rochester. Read in full as the PDF in the university's research repository. The source for the account of Frankena's argument, with Frankena's page numbers as the thesis gives them, and it argues against Frankena rather than for him.

Curry, O. (2006). Who's Afraid of the Naturalistic Fallacy? Evolutionary Psychology, 4(1), 234-247. Read in full as the PDF deposited in the Oxford University Research Archive. The source for the eight uses of the name and for the quotations from Evans and Buss, both of which are quoted here at one remove through it.
Naturalistic Fallacy. Logically Fallacious, accessed 16 August 2026. Cited as an instance of current popular usage, in which the is-ought reading comes first and Moore's comes second.
Naturalistic fallacy. English Wikipedia, accessed 16 August 2026. Cited for its opening definition and for traffic, 44,259 views in 2025 by the Wikimedia pageviews API.

Alfano, M., Machery, E., Plakias, A., & Loeb, D. Experimental Moral Philosophy. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, first published 19 March 2014, substantive revision 29 June 2022. Read in full from the page source to establish that it discusses neither the open question argument nor the naturalistic fallacy.

Daston, L. (2014). The Naturalistic Fallacy Is Modern. Isis, 105(3), 579-587. Verified at Crossref. Located while searching for a history of the term, closed at the publisher, and not obtained. Nothing on this page rests on it.
